title: Race Cars Zoom Past Museums: Will the Art Be Okay?
summary:
Imagine a race car zooming past a museum at 180 miles per hour! That's what's happening this weekend in Washington, D.C. More than two dozen IndyCar drivers will race 147 laps around the National Mall for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix. The track is 1.7 miles long and goes right past famous places like the National Gallery of Art, the National Archives, and the Smithsonian's Air and Space Museum.

But here's the big question: could the loud, fast cars shake the buildings and damage the art inside? The National Gallery of Art has a sculpture garden along the track. They boarded up some outdoor sculptures to keep them safe. A spokesperson said they did a big vibration study and are taking steps to protect everything.

Race organizers say they are being very careful. They point to other races in special places, like one in Detroit's Belle Isle Park and another that goes past the Dali Museum in Florida. The Dali Museum was built to survive a Category 5 hurricane, so they're not worried.

But some people are still nervous. Art historian Mary Okin says the National Mall is different. Usually, cars go only 25 mph there. This is the first time a big race has ever been held on the Mall. She worries about vibrations, fires, or flying debris. "For several hours of racing cars, we might be risking the access to these extraordinary works for future generations," she said.

The race is part of the country's big birthday celebration. It will be exciting to watch, but everyone hopes the art stays safe too.
why_it_matters: It shows how fun public events can create real worries about protecting museums that kids may visit on school trips and that future generations should get to enjoy.
